name: Refugee Council: therapeutic services (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: refugees and people seeking asylum in England, helped where they live now.
summary: The Refugee Council's Therapeutic Services (£1.74m in the year to March 2025) gave one-to-one, group, child and family therapy to 303 refugees and people seeking asylum who had been through trauma, plus an uncounted number of children in its MyView service (judged about 50). The effect is the Cochrane-method review of psychosocial interventions for refugees (Turrini et al. 2019: about 1 SD on depression against waitlist or usual care), fading over about a year and a half, cut to about 0.3 of that by trust in small heterogeneous trials, what clients would have got anyway, the Refugee Council's share of the credit and incomplete courses, plus the suicides it averts. It comes to about 0.003 years of healthy life per $1,000 (combined range 0.0004-0.016), low because each person costs about $7,000 and a WELLBY is worth a fifteenth of a healthy year at the site's rate. The branch is discounted for missing data (no evaluation of the Refugee Council's own therapy, which mixes psychotherapy, art and music therapy and groups rather than the trials' protocols); the biggest uncertainties are how much of the trials' effect carries over and how long it lasts.

source.title: British Refugee Council (Refugee Council), Trustees Annual Report and Accounts for the year ended 31 March 2025 (audited; Charity Commission register, charity 1014576)
source.quote: our highly experienced, specialist teams were able to provide therapeutic support to 303 refugees

rows.explainer: The report's count for the Refugee Services' therapy teams (Ukrainian groups, child and family therapy, Lewisham).

rows.label: Children and young people in MyView therapy, not in the count above
rows.explainer: Judgment 50 (0-200): MyView, the therapy service for children who arrive alone (psychotherapy, art and music therapy, p. 8), is described in the children's section with no count, and the accounts don't say which line pays its therapists. If Children's Services pays it, its children are counted here against a cost that isn't (the low end, 0, removes them; charityevals' services model counts those children's general advice gain only, not therapy). The Therapeutic Services line costs about £5,700 for each of the 303 counted, several times a course of therapy (15 sessions at £100-150 is £1,500-2,250), which suggests some clients beyond the count: 50, between the two readings.

rows.label: Cost per person
rows.explainer: Context: several thousand dollars a person; charityevals' Wounded Warrior Project mental health model about $11,000.

rows.label: Effect on depression at the end of therapy (SD)

source.title: Turrini et al. 2019, Efficacy and acceptability of psychosocial interventions in asylum seekers and refugees: systematic review and meta-analysis, Epidemiology and Psychiatric Sciences 28(4):376-388
source.quote: depression (SMD = −1.02; 95% CI −1.52 to −0.51; I2 = 89%; 95% CI 82 –93; 12 studies, 844 participants; moderate quality evidence)

rows.explainer: The pooled effect of psychosocial interventions for asylum seekers and refugees with psychological distress on depressive symptoms, 12 randomised trials, 844 participants, mostly trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy, against waitlist or usual care; its 95% CI is the range. The depression scale is the one the site's WELLBYs per SD-year are measured on. No prediction interval is published; the pooled interval understates the spread between settings (I² 89%), which evidence_adj takes up.

rows.label: Years until the effect has faded to nothing

source.title: Turrini et al. 2019, Efficacy and acceptability of psychosocial interventions in asylum seekers and refugees: systematic review and meta-analysis, Epidemiology and Psychiatric Sciences 28(4):376-388
source.quote: This beneficial effect was maintained at 1 month or longer follow-up

rows.explainer: Judgment 1.5 years (9 months to 3 years) for a straight fade: the review found the effect maintained at follow-ups of a month or more (depression SMD 1.28 in 8 studies), but the follow-ups are short; refugees' continuing stresses (asylum decisions, housing, separation) wear gains away. charityevals' Wounded Warrior Project model takes 4.2 years for veterans' trauma therapy with a measured one-year follow-up; shorter here because the evidence is shorter and clients' circumstances are less settled.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)

source.title: Turrini et al. 2019, Efficacy and acceptability of psychosocial interventions in asylum seekers and refugees: systematic review and meta-analysis, Epidemiology and Psychiatric Sciences 28(4):376-388
source.quote: Removing the five studies with outlier results (Hinton et al., 2004, 2005, 2009; Acarturk et al., 2015, 2016) the overall estimate remained significant (SMD = −0.33

rows.explainer: Judgment 0.5 (0.3-0.75). Internal: small trials with lack of blinding, high heterogeneity, and five outlier trials whose removal more than halves the PTSD effect (0.71 to 0.33 SD); about 0.6. External, for population and setting only: the trials' refugees are similar, but many of the Refugee Council's clients are still in the asylum system with its continuing stresses; about 0.85. That the therapies delivered aren't the trials' protocols is the missing-data step's question, not counted here. After this, the counterfactual, the share of credit and delivery, the effect counted is about 0.3 of the review's 1.02 SD (0.15 with the missing-data discount). Anchor: charityevals' Wounded Warrior Project model takes 0.6 for trials of the very therapies it delivers.

rows.label: Share of the effect that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Judgment 90% (70-100%): the trials' effect is already against waitlist or usual care, which in high-income settings includes access to public mental-health services. Below 1 only for clients who would have got specialist trauma therapy elsewhere and the trials' controls didn't: NHS Talking Therapies take self-referrals, but refugees reach them less (language, waiting lists, people moved between asylum hotels). No access rate for refugees is published; anchor: charityevals' Wounded Warrior Project model takes 0.7 for veterans with free VA trauma therapy on offer, higher here where specialist care is harder to reach.

rows.label: The Refugee Council's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Judgment 90% (75-100%): interpreters, GPs who refer and partner organisations contribute; the NHS grant is the Refugee Council's own income and is in the cost.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (dose, completion)
rows.explainer: Judgment 75% (60-90%): some clients get a few group sessions rather than a full course (Fatima had fifteen individual sessions, p. 13); dropout is common when people are moved between asylum accommodation.

rows.label: Counted less for missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin: clients counted (the MyView children judged), but the therapies delivered aren't the trials' protocols and there is no evaluation of them. Counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Side effects: better functioning and parenting beyond the depression effect
rows.explainer: +3% (-2 to +8%): less anxiety and PTSD beyond what the depression scale captures is mostly the same change; better sleep, school attendance for the children and parents' care of their children add a little (the review's functioning and quality-of-life outcomes trended positive but weren't significant). No harm found in the trials; therapy that reopens trauma without follow-up could do some (the low end).

rows.label: Yearly suicide rate of the population treated

source.title: Office for National Statistics, Suicides in England and Wales: 2023 registrations
source.quote: There were 6,069 suicides registered in England and Wales (11.4 deaths per 100,000 people) in 2023

rows.explainer: England and Wales's age-standardised rate in 2023, 11.4 per 100,000 (17.4 for men). Refugees' own rate in the UK is not published. The range runs from the female-heavy groups (lower) to young men in insecure status (higher).

rows.label: Relative risk of suicide with depression
rows.explainer: The shared figure for depression's excess suicide risk (facts/depression.json), 5 (2-15): the meta-analysis of Harris and Barraclough (1997, British Journal of Psychiatry 170:205-228, doi:10.1192/bjp.170.3.205) puts it at about 20 for treated major depression, community samples at about 2-3; clients of trauma services are a mix of severity, between the two.

rows.label: Share of the excess suicide risk removed at the end of therapy
rows.explainer: Judgment 20% (5-40%): trials of psychological therapy rarely show fewer suicides directly; the risk is taken to fall in proportion to part of the symptom change. As charityevals' Wounded Warrior Project model (30%, 10-60%), lower here for a smaller effect counted.

rows.label: Suicides averted per person treated
rows.explainer: The site's recipe (templates.md, wellbeing): yearly rate × the excess risk × the share removed, over the effect's years as it fades, discounted like the WELLBYs.

rows.label: Share of the suicides averted aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: Judgment 88% (75-95%): the clients are mostly young adults and teenagers; the rest 50-74.

rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights for the clients' age bands, times your value of a life.
